svg.font-family: Inter, Segoe UI, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: Figure 2. Where attacker effort moved once sign in got harder
svg.desc: Two observed attacks against the recovery and fallback path rather than against authentication itself. The first is the downgrade: a phishing kit responsible for a majority of blocked phishing volume in 2025 carried code that detects a passkey prompt and steers the target to a weaker method that can be relayed. The second is the help desk: a criminal group documented by national agencies telephones support, impersonates an employee, and has the password reset and the second factor moved to a device it controls. A band below gives the design conclusion, which is that adding a strong method to a system that still offers a weak recovery route does not make the system phishing resistant.
svg.text: Hardening the sign in did not reduce the number of attackers. It relocated them, and both of these are observed in the wild rather than predicted.
do not beat the strong method, offer a weaker one

g.text: A phishing kit sold as a service, credited with the
majority of the phishing volume one large provider
blocked in mid 2025, carries code for this.
It detects that the real site is about to ask for a
passkey, and steers the target to a different method.
Nothing about the passkey was defeated. It was simply
never used, because a plausible page said the fingerprint
reader was unavailable and offered a code instead.
Why this is the lesson and not a footnote
Every fallback you leave enabled is a menu item the
attacker gets to choose from, and the attacker will
always choose the worst one you left on.

svg.text: do not attack the account, attack the person who can reset it

g.text: A criminal group documented in a joint national advisory,
first in 2023 and updated in July 2025, works this way
as its primary route in.
It telephones support, presents itself as an employee,
and has the password reset and the second factor moved
to a device it controls.
No malware, no phishing page, and no interaction with
the target at all. The target finds out afterwards.
What the advisory recommends is instructive
Scripted identity checks, two independent verifications
with one of them resistant to voice impersonation, and
resets correlated against ticket evidence.

svg.text: The conclusion both of these point at, stated at a standards conference in 2025
Adding passkeys as an option does not make a system phishing resistant, if a text message recovery or a password reset path is still there.
Which is the argument from Lesson 4.3, arriving from the other direction: adding a strong method raises nothing while a weak one is still reachable.
What this means for you specifically, as somebody who will be on both sides of it

g.text: On your own accounts: the audit in this lesson is a search for menu items you forgot you left on. Most people find at least two.
On an engagement: the recovery path is scope that clients routinely forget to think about, and the help desk is part of the attack surface.

svg.text: Neither of these attacks touches your password, your key, or your vault. Both of them end with the attacker signed in as you.
